gaps.sentence: The man ___ lives next door is a doctor.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' refers to people as the subject of the clause; 'which' is for things and 'whose' shows possession.

gaps.sentence: Students ___ hand in their essays late will lose marks.
gaps.explanation: 'Who' refers to the students performing the action; the verb 'will lose' follows later in the sentence.

gaps.sentence: The village ___ my grandmother was born has no shops.
gaps.explanation: 'Where' is the relative adverb for places; 'which' cannot stand alone here because no preposition is present.

gaps.sentence: It is one of the most impressive buildings ___ I have ever seen.
gaps.explanation: After superlative expressions, 'that' is the standard relative pronoun in defining clauses.

gaps.sentence: The 1990s was the decade ___ mobile phones became common.
gaps.explanation: 'When' replaces 'in which' after time nouns; 'which' cannot stand alone here.

gaps.sentence: The manager, for ___ the team played so hard, thanked everyone.
gaps.hint: played for the manager — person after preposition
gaps.explanation: The preposition 'for' demands the object form 'whom' for a person.

gaps.sentence: That's the boy ___ dog won first prize at the show.
gaps.hint: the dog belongs to the boy
gaps.explanation: 'Whose dog' means 'his dog'; 'who's' would mean 'who is', which makes no sense here.

gaps.sentence: The Blue Train, ___ runs between Pretoria and Cape Town, is famous for its luxury.
gaps.explanation: For a thing in a non-defining clause use 'which'; 'that' cannot follow the comma.
